name: primecount
desc: Fast prime counting function program and C/C++ library
why: Fast prime counting via combinatorial algorithms, real number theory software you can run to count primes far beyond brute force.

brief.what_it_is: primecount is a command-line program and C/C++ library that counts the primes up to x, for x up to 10^31. You give it a number, such as 1e14, and it prints pi(x), the count of primes less than or equal to x. It can also compute the nth prime (--nth-prime), approximate pi(x) with Riemann R or Li functions, and evaluate phi(x, a). It is built on the combinatorial prime counting algorithms, parallelized with OpenMP.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a program built on highly optimized implementations of the combinatorial prime counting algorithms, so you can count primes far beyond what brute-force sieving can reach. It also says it contains the first open source implementations of the Deleglise-Rivat algorithm and Xavier Gourdon's algorithm.
brief.how_it_works: It implements Legendre, Meissel, Lehmer, Lagarias-Miller-Odlyzko, Deleglise-Rivat and Gourdon formulas, which reduce pi(x) to a sum of phi function values and correction terms (P2, S1, S2, and others) evaluated over a small sieve bound. The default is Gourdon's algorithm. Its nth-prime method estimates the nth prime with the inverse Li or inverse R function, counts primes up to that guess, then runs a segmented sieve forward to the exact answer. A custom load balancer is shared across implementations and, per the README, scales to hundreds of CPU cores.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install primecount, the README lists winget install primecount on Windows, pacman, apt, dnf, zypper and pkg install on Arch, Debian/Ubuntu, Fedora, openSUSE and FreeBSD. For development against libprimecount, install libprimecount-dev or libprimecount-devel. To build from source you need a C++ compiler and CMake; the README recommends GCC or Clang because they support both OpenMP and 128-bit integers. Detailed build instructions are in doc/BUILD.md. No accounts or hardware requirements are mentioned.
brief.standout: It claims the first open source implementations of Deleglise-Rivat and Gourdon's algorithm, and a novel shared load balancer that scales to hundreds of cores. Its hard special leaves use a linear counter array with POPCNT in place of a binary indexed tree, which the author says is more cache efficient. Bindings exist for Python, Julia, Rust, Haskell, Lua and Common Lisp.
brief.status: Appears maintained, but the README gives no release date or commit date, so this is not confirmed. Evidence: CI and benchmark workflow badges, benchmarks run on a 2025 AMD EPYC Zen5 CPU, a sponsors section where the author says donations motivate continued maintenance, and packages across many distributions.
brief.caveats: Maximum input is 10^31. The benchmark table covers x from 10^10 to 10^22; Legendre, Meissel and LMO show NaN from 10^19 upward, so those results are not reported. The README says Gourdon's advantage over Deleglise-Rivat should not be read as solely the algorithm's advantage, since the Gourdon implementation includes newer improvements. Building from source needs CMake and ideally GCC or Clang for OpenMP and 128-bit integers. The bindings section of the README says 'primesieve natively supports C and C++', which appears to be a copy-paste error for primecount. The brew caveats field was empty.
